title: After Sikh Grandmother's Deportation, Bill Would Let Old Removal Orders Expire
excerpt: Four California Democrats introduced the Protect Our Neighbors Act on Thursday, citing Harjit Kaur, 73, who reported to ICE every six months for over 13 years before she was detained at a routine check-in and deported to India.
body:
• Four California Democrats in the US House — John Garamendi, Lateefah Simon, Zoe Lofgren and Juan Vargas — introduced the Protect Our Neighbors Act on Thursday, November 19, to protect long-term immigrant residents who have lived in the United States for over 10 years.
  • The bill would make final removal orders expire 10 years after issuance for people who have been continuously present in the US and have not been convicted of a crime, and would open a pathway to lawful permanent residency once an order expires.
  • The legislation was inspired by Harjit Kaur, a 73-year-old Sikh grandmother who lived in the US for over 30 years, reported to ICE every six months for more than 13 years, and was detained at a routine check-in in September 2025 and deported to India.
  • Nothing changes yet for the roughly 1.19 million people living in the US with removal orders: this is a newly introduced bill, not law, and no application under it exists.

Four California Democrats in the US House of Representatives introduced legislation on Thursday that would let old deportation orders expire and give long-settled immigrants a route to legal status. The Protect Our Neighbors Act, announced by Representatives John Garamendi, Lateefah Simon, Zoe Lofgren and Juan Vargas, is built around the case of one of their constituents: Harjit Kaur, a 73-year-old Sikh grandmother deported to India last year after more than three decades in the United States.

The case behind the bill

Kaur had lived in the US since the early 1990s and was a constituent of Garamendi; she worked for decades in Simon's district, as a seamstress at Sari Palace in Berkeley, according to the East Bay Times. Her asylum case was denied in 2012. She had no criminal record, and for more than 13 years she complied with the condition ICE set for her: reporting to immigration officials every six months.

On September 8, 2025, she was detained during one of those routine check-ins and held at an ICE facility in Bakersfield, according to Garamendi's office. At around 2:00 a.m. on September 19, she was transported in handcuffs to Los Angeles, flown to Georgia without notice to her family or attorney, and placed on a charter flight to India — deported before her family, who had arranged to travel with her, could say goodbye. Garamendi's office said Kaur had sought travel documents from the Indian Consulate but was reportedly turned away multiple times; she had not refused to return, but could not depart without valid documents. During detention, the office said, she was held without a bed and forced to sleep on the floor, shackled during transfers, and denied vegetarian meals, adequate food, water and medication.

"We are still traumatized and horrified by the cruel treatment of our grandmother one year ago. Harjit was a pillar to our family and our community."

— Harjit Kaur's family, in a statement released by the sponsors

What the bill would change

A final order of removal is a formal legal order requiring a noncitizen to leave the US, but it does not always mean immediate removal: removal can be delayed through deferred action, a stay or ongoing litigation. According to the American Immigration Council, roughly 1.19 million people with removal orders remain in the US, many of them for years. Under the current administration, Garamendi's office said, DHS and ICE have aggressively pursued people with final orders regardless of how long removal had been deferred, putting long-term residents who routinely complied with check-ins at renewed risk.

The bill would establish a 10-year expiration on final orders of removal for individuals who have been continuously present in the US and have not been convicted of a crime. Counted here: people whose removal orders are more than 10 years old and who meet the presence and clean-record conditions. Not counted: anyone convicted of an offence punishable by more than a year in prison, who could not use the bill's route to status. An immigration judge could renew an expired order at the Homeland Security Secretary's request, but only with clear and convincing evidence of significant reasons for the delay unrelated to administrative or funding problems, and new evidence that renewal served the public interest; renewal would be barred while a person's status petition was pending, according to reports of the published bill text.

For people whose orders expire unrenewed, the bill would amend the Immigration and Nationality Act to create a pathway to lawful permanent residency. Applications would require a fee capped at $1,200 and a certified copy of the applicant's latest federal income-tax return. Neither the expiration of an order nor an application would automatically confer a green card. The sponsors describe the package as bicameral; Kaur's family thanked Senator Adam Schiff alongside the House sponsors for their advocacy.

What it means if you have an old removal order

For now, nothing. The Act was introduced on Thursday and would have to pass both chambers of Congress and be signed before any of its provisions take effect. Removal orders remain enforceable, check-in obligations remain in force, and there is no form to file under this bill. Readers in that position should keep attending scheduled ICE check-ins and take advice from an immigration attorney rather than from anyone offering to file under a law that does not yet exist. The next steps to watch are the bill's committee referral and whether the Senate companion moves.
